introduction.title: Mind-Body Approaches to Healing
introduction.description: Evidence-based techniques that address the connection between emotions, beliefs, and physical symptoms. These approaches recognize that unprocessed emotions, limiting beliefs, and chronic stress can manifest as physical symptoms, and that addressing the psychological components can support healing.
introduction.note: These practices are complementary tools for self-exploration and emotional processing. They are not substitutes for medical care when dealing with serious conditions, persistent symptoms, or trauma.

journalSpeak.title: JournalSpeak
journalSpeak.creator: Nicole Sachs, LCSW
journalSpeak.source: Based on Dr. John Sarno's mind-body work
journalSpeak.description: A structured expressive journaling practice designed to help process unresolved emotions that may be contributing to physical symptoms. The method involves writing about emotional stressors without censorship, followed by self-soothing meditation.
journalSpeak.background: JournalSpeak builds on the work of Dr. John Sarno, who proposed that many chronic pain conditions (especially back, neck, and shoulder pain) can be driven by repressed emotions—primarily anger, fear, and anxiety. Sarno called this Tension Myositis Syndrome (TMS) or mind-body syndrome. When the unconscious mind suppresses difficult emotions, the body may create physical symptoms as a distraction. By bringing these emotions into conscious awareness through writing, the symptoms often diminish.

step1_lists.title: Create Your Lists
step1_lists.description: Start by creating three foundational lists that will serve as writing prompts.

pastStressors.title: Past Stressors
pastStressors.description: Events from your past (childhood through adulthood) that caused stress, fear, anger, guilt, shame, or humiliation.
examples: Lack of affection or emotional support
Addiction or mental illness in the family
Being an energetic mismatch with caregivers
Any event that means something to you, even if others wouldn't understand

currentStressors.title: Current Stressors
currentStressors.description: Ongoing sources of stress in your present life.
examples: Specific relationships (name each person: family, friends, colleagues)
Job, career, or sense of purpose
Pain, symptoms, or diagnoses and their impact on your life
Regret or resentment related to your health journey
Any unresolved issues from your Past Stressors list

personalityTraits.title: Personality Traits
personalityTraits.description: Aspects of your personality that may contribute to stress or emotional repression.
examples: Needing approval or validation from others
Putting others' needs before your own

step2_write.title: Write for 20 Minutes
step2_write.description: Pick any topic from your lists and write continuously for at least 20 minutes.
guidelines: Don't overthink where to start—just pick one and begin
If you go off on a tangent, follow it (like a bunny exploring in the snow)
20 minutes is the minimum to move past resistance; you can write longer if needed
Write the raw, unfiltered truth—no censorship, no editing
Nobody else will read this (consider deleting or destroying it afterward)
Think of it as 'word vomit' or a tantrum on paper
Focus on how you FEEL, not just the facts of what happened
Notice what's happening in your body as you write
Invite difficult emotions to surface (they may not come right away—that's okay)
The goal is to express hidden, unfelt feelings so they're no longer stuck in your body
step2_write.privacyNote: JournalSpeak entries are meant to be private, cathartic releases. Many practitioners recommend deleting or destroying the writing after completing the practice to reinforce that this is for processing, not preserving.

step3_meditate.title: Self-Soothing Meditation (10 Minutes)
step3_meditate.description: After writing, transition to a calming meditation to soothe your nervous system and support re-entry into daily life.
options: Any gentle, grounding practice that feels supportive
step3_meditate.purpose: Meditation and self-compassion are essential companions to JournalSpeak. After expressing difficult emotions, you need to offer yourself kindness and forgiveness.

step4_repeat.title: Practice Regularly
step4_repeat.description: The most effective approach is to practice JournalSpeak daily, especially when beginning this work.
benefits: Reduces internal stress and nervous system activation
Moves you from fight-or-flight into rest-and-repair
Builds capacity to feel and process difficult emotions

journalSpeak.whenToUse: JournalSpeak is particularly helpful for chronic pain, unexplained physical symptoms, tension and stress-related conditions, and when you feel stuck emotionally. It's a practice, not a quick fix—consistency over time brings the most benefit.

sarnoTMS.title: Dr. Sarno's TMS Concepts
sarnoTMS.creator: Dr. John E. Sarno, MD
sarnoTMS.description: Tension Myositis Syndrome (TMS), also called mind-body syndrome, refers to physical symptoms—especially chronic pain—that are caused by repressed emotions rather than structural damage.

coreIdeas.premise: Many chronic pain conditions (back, neck, shoulder, headaches, digestive issues, etc.) arise when the unconscious mind creates physical symptoms to distract from unbearable emotions like rage, anxiety, fear, or shame.
coreIdeas.mechanism: Sarno originally proposed that the brain restricts blood flow to muscles and nerves, causing pain. While current pain science doesn't support that specific mechanism, research does confirm that the brain can generate and amplify pain in response to psychological factors.
coreIdeas.emotionalRoot: The pain serves as a defense mechanism—your conscious mind focuses on the body, preventing overwhelming emotions from surfacing.
treatment: Education: Understanding that the pain is real but generated by the brain, not by structural damage
Emotional awareness: Identifying and processing repressed emotions through journaling or therapy
Resuming activity: Gradually returning to normal physical activity to retrain the brain
Rejecting the structural diagnosis: Letting go of fear-based beliefs about fragility or damage

sarnoTMS.note: TMS is not a mainstream medical diagnosis. However, related concepts like Pain Reprocessing Therapy have been validated in randomized controlled trials. If you have unexplained chronic pain, this perspective may be worth exploring alongside appropriate medical care.

expressiveWriting.title: Expressive Writing (Pennebaker Method)
expressiveWriting.creator: Dr. James Pennebaker
expressiveWriting.description: A research-backed writing practice where you write about traumatic or stressful experiences for 15-20 minutes on 3-5 occasions. Studies show improvements in mental and physical health compared to neutral writing.

protocol.frequency: 3-5 sessions (can be consecutive days or spread out)
protocol.topic: Write about a traumatic, stressful, or emotional experience
guidelines: Write continuously without worrying about grammar or spelling
Explore your deepest thoughts and feelings about the event
Connect the experience to your relationships, life story, or identity
Use insight words (realize, understand, because) and causal words (caused, led to, resulted in)
The goal is to create a coherent narrative that helps you make sense of the experience

benefits: Helpful for trauma survivors (though not a substitute for therapy)

painReprocessingTherapy.title: Pain Reprocessing Therapy (PRT)
painReprocessingTherapy.description: A psychological treatment system designed to rewire the brain and break the cycle of chronic pain. PRT teaches that many chronic pain conditions are driven by learned neural pathways rather than ongoing tissue damage.
components: Education: Understanding the brain origins and reversibility of pain
Evidence gathering: Collecting personalized proof that your pain is brain-generated
Somatic tracking: Attending to pain sensations through a lens of safety (not threat)
Addressing emotional threats: Identifying and processing fear, anxiety, and other emotions
Positive focus: Gravitating toward positive feelings and sensations
painReprocessingTherapy.research: A 2021 randomized controlled trial (published in JAMA Psychiatry) found that 66% of participants were pain-free or nearly pain-free after PRT treatment, compared to 20% in the placebo group.
painReprocessingTherapy.relatedResource: The Curable app offers PRT exercises, neuroscience education, guided meditations, and expressive writing prompts for chronic pain conditions.
painReprocessingTherapy.conditions: PRT has been used for chronic back pain, migraines, fibromyalgia, sciatica, nerve pain, IBS, tension headaches, and other conditions lasting 6+ months with no clear tissue damage.

ifsPartsWork.title: Internal Family Systems (IFS) / Parts Work
ifsPartsWork.creator: Dr. Richard Schwartz
ifsPartsWork.description: IFS views the mind as a family of inner parts—each with its own perspective, feelings, and role. The goal is to get to know these parts with curiosity and compassion, helping them heal and work together under the leadership of Self.

parts.managers: Protective parts that try to keep you safe by controlling your environment, people-pleasing, perfectionism, planning, or being critical.
parts.firefighters: Reactive protectors that jump in when emotions become overwhelming—through distraction, numbing, impulsive behavior, or dissociation.
parts.exiles: Wounded, often younger parts that carry pain, shame, fear, or trauma. Protectors try to keep exiles hidden to avoid overwhelming you.

coreConcepts.self: Your core essence—calm, compassionate, curious, confident, creative, clear, courageous, and connected. Self can lead the system and heal the parts.
coreConcepts.the6Fs: A process for getting to know a part: Find it, Focus on it, Flesh it out, Feel toward it (with curiosity), beFriend it, and explore its Fears.

howToUse: Notice when a part is present (e.g., a critical voice, anxiety, procrastination)
Turn your attention inward and find where it lives in your body
Ask how you feel toward the part (if it's anything other than curious or compassionate, another part is blended—ask it to step back)
Get to know the part: What's its job? What's it protecting you from? What does it fear would happen if it stopped?
Listen without judgment, building trust and letting the part feel seen
ifsPartsWork.note: IFS is a therapeutic model, often practiced with a trained therapist. Self-exploration is possible, but deep trauma work should be done with professional support.

eftTapping.title: Emotional Freedom Technique (EFT) / Tapping
eftTapping.creator: Gary Craig (based on Thought Field Therapy by Roger Callahan)
eftTapping.description: A self-help technique combining cognitive focus on a specific stressor with gentle tapping on acupressure points. Used to reduce stress, anxiety, and difficult emotions.

protocol.step1: Identify the issue or emotion you want to address
protocol.step2: Rate its intensity on a scale of 0-10
protocol.step3: Create a setup statement: 'Even though [issue], I deeply and completely accept myself'
protocol.step4: Tap on the side of your hand (karate chop point) while repeating the setup statement 3 times
protocol.step5: Tap through the sequence (7-9 taps per point) while stating the issue:
tappingPoints: Side of the eye (on the bone)
Under the arm (about 4 inches below armpit)
protocol.step6: Rate the intensity again—repeat as needed until it decreases

eftTapping.evidence: Studies show EFT can reduce anxiety and depression symptoms, though most research relies on self-reported outcomes. It's considered safe as a complementary tool.
eftTapping.note: EFT should not replace therapy for serious depression, trauma, or PTSD. If emotions feel overwhelming, reach out to a mental health professional.

theWork.title: The Work of Byron Katie
theWork.creator: Byron Katie
theWork.description: A simple yet powerful inquiry method for questioning stressful thoughts. The Work helps you examine beliefs that cause suffering and discover turnarounds that offer new perspectives.

process.step1: Identify a stressful thought or judgment (e.g., 'She doesn't respect me' or 'I should be further along by now')
fourQuestions: Can you absolutely know that it's true?
How do you react—what happens—when you believe that thought?
Who or what would you be without the thought?
process.step3: Turn the thought around: Find opposites of the original statement

turnarounds.toSelf: 'She doesn't respect me' → 'I don't respect me' (or 'I don't respect her')
turnarounds.toOther: 'She doesn't respect me' → 'I don't respect her'
turnarounds.toOpposite: 'She doesn't respect me' → 'She does respect me'

process.step4: Find at least three genuine examples of how each turnaround is as true or truer than the original thought

theWork.purpose: The Work is a meditation on reality. It helps you see that suffering comes not from reality itself, but from your thoughts about reality. When you question those thoughts, you often find peace.
theWork.note: The Work is a tool for self-inquiry, not a replacement for therapy or medical care. It works best when you're genuinely curious about your own beliefs.
